draft.title: The conscription referendums
card: Conscription means the government requires people to serve in the military. In 1916 Australia's volunteer army needed more soldiers, as casualties were high and fewer men were enlisting.
Prime Minister Billy Hughes asked voters to allow conscription for overseas service. He held a referendum, a national vote, in October 1916 and another in December 1917.
Both referendums were defeated, so Australia's soldiers stayed volunteers. The votes were close, and the second was lost by a larger margin than the first.
The issue split the nation. Families, churches, unions, political parties and even Hughes's own Labor Party were divided, and Hughes was expelled from Labor.
draft.remember: Hughes asked twice, voters said no twice, and the argument divided Australians.

a.q: What did Prime Minister Hughes ask voters to decide in 1916 and 1917?
opts: Whether men could be required to serve overseas
Whether Australia should join the war at all
Whether soldiers should be paid more by the government
Whether Australia should leave the British Empire
a.why: Both referendums asked if the government could require men to serve overseas. They did not ask about joining the war, which had already begun, and they were not about pay.

b.q: Mei's great-grandfather was a Labor supporter in Brisbane in 1917. His brother, also a Labor supporter, voted the opposite way in the referendum. What does this show about the issue?
opts: It divided families and even supporters of one party
It united Labor supporters behind one clear view
It was decided by the government without a vote
It mattered only to people living in the cities
b.why: Brothers who supported the same party voted differently, which shows how deeply the issue split people. It was not settled without a vote, because Hughes held referendums. The idea that Labor supporters were united is wrong, as the party itself was divided.
b.clue: Both brothers supported the same party but disagreed.

a.best: Whether men could be required to serve overseas

b.best: It divided families and even supporters of one party

check.summary: No problems found. The dates, the larger 1917 'No' margin, the Labor split and Hughes's expulsion all check out, and both questions have one clear right answer.
